1F (Number Theory)

Words: 151 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 151
1F OurBigBook.com
For an odd composite N and a unit b modulo N, N is a Fermat pseudoprime to base b when
bN−1≡1(modN).
(1)
It is an Euler pseudoprime to base b when
b(N−1)/2≡(Nb​)(modN),
(2)
where the right side is the Jacobi symbol.
By the Chinese remainder theorem,
(Z/105Z)×≅(Z/3Z)××(Z/5Z)××(Z/7Z)×,
(3)
and φ(105)=2⋅4⋅6=48. The condition b104=1 is automatic modulo 3 and 5. Modulo 7 it has
gcd(104,6)=2
(4)
solutions. Thus there are 2⋅4⋅2=16 Fermat bases, giving proportion
4816​=31​​.
(5)
For the Euler condition, b52=1 modulo 3, so the Jacobi symbol must be +1. The power condition is automatic modulo 5, while modulo 7 it again restricts b to the two solutions of b2=1. For each of those two residues, exactly half of the 2⋅4 choices modulo 3 and 5 have Jacobi symbol +1. Hence there are 2⋅4=8 Euler bases and proportion
488​=61​​.
(6)

The nth Chebyshev polynomial is defined on [−1,1] by
Tn​(x)=cos(narccosx).
(7)
The cosine addition formula gives
T0​(x)=1,T1​(x)=x,Tn+1​(x)=2xTn​(x)−Tn−1​(x).
(8)
Induction therefore shows that every Tn​ is a polynomial. Its defining cosine formula also gives
−1≤Tn​(x)≤1(−1≤x≤1)​.
(9)

The assertion is clear for T1​=x. If Tn​ has degree n and leading coefficient 2n−1, the recurrence shows that the leading term of Tn+1​ is
2x⋅2n−1xn=2nxn+1;
(10)
the lower-degree polynomial Tn−1​ cannot cancel it. Hence
lc(Tn​)=2n−1(n≥1)​.
(11)

For x=cosθ∈[−1,1],
Tn​(−x)=cos(n(π−θ))=(−1)ncos(nθ)=(−1)nTn​(x).
(12)
Both sides are polynomials in x. Since they agree on an interval, the polynomial identity theorem extends the equality to every real x. Thus Tn​ is even for even n and odd for odd n.

Words: 65 Articles: 1

Solution

d OurBigBook.com
The n roots of Tn​ are distinct and lie in (−1,1). Repeated use of Rolle's theorem shows that every root of Tn(k)​, for 0≤k<n, also lies in (−1,1). Its leading coefficient is positive, so
Tn(k)​(x)>0(x≥1).
(13)
Taking k=r+1 shows that
dxd​Tn(r)​(x)=Tn(r+1)​(x)>0
(14)
for 0≤r≤n−1; when r=n−1, the derivative is the positive constant Tn(n)​. This is the positivity of Chebyshev derivatives beyond the unit interval.

Tn′​(1)=limθ→0​sinθnsin(nθ)​=n2.

Tn​(x)−Tn​(1)=∫1x​Tn′​(t)dt≥n2(x−1).
(16)
Since Tn​(1)=1 and n2≥n,
Tn​(x)≥1+n(x−1)(x≥1)​.

3K (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 65 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 65
3K OurBigBook.com
Binary Huffman coding repeatedly merges the two least probable current symbols, assigns opposite bits to the two children of every merge, and reads each original symbol's codeword from the root. The resulting prefix code minimizes expected word length.
The merge weights here may be chosen as
.02+.03=.05,.04+.04=.08,.05+.08=.13,.12+.13=.25,.25+.26=.51,.49+.51=1.
(18)
One corresponding code is
code​x1​0​x2​10​x3​110​x4​11110​x5​11111​x6​11101​x7​11100.​​
(19)
Its expected word length is
.49+2(.26)+3(.12)+5(.04+.04+.03+.02)=2.02​.
(20)

Take the productions
S→AA,A→a,
(21)
and the word w=aa. There is only one parse tree: its root uses S→AA and each child uses A→a. There are nevertheless exactly two derivations,
S⇒AA⇒aA⇒aa
(22)
and
S⇒AA⇒Aa⇒aa,
(23)
according as the left or right occurrence of A is replaced first. This illustrates that derivations record replacement order while a context-free grammar parse tree does not.

Words: 162 Articles: 1
4J OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 162
c OurBigBook.com
Assume that L is context-free and let p be its pumping length. Apply the pumping lemma for context-free languages to
w=apbpap.
(28)
Write w=uvxyz, with ∣vxy∣≤p and ∣vy∣>0. The substring vxy meets at most two of the three constant-letter blocks.
If v and y affect only the first block, only the middle block, or only the last block, pumping down immediately makes the final block length differ from the minimum of the first two lengths. If they meet the first and second blocks, pumping down decreases at least one of those block lengths while leaving the final length p, again violating the defining minimum.
It remains that they meet the second and third blocks. Let pumping change their lengths by s and t, respectively. Pumping down fails unless s=t. If s=t>0, pumping up gives lengths
p,p+s,p+s,
(29)
whose last entry is not min(p,p+s)=p. Thus some pumping exponent always leaves L, contradicting the lemma. Hence
L is not context-free​.
(30)

a OurBigBook.com
For F(n)=αn−βn3, the nonnegative equilibria are
n=0,n=K:=α/β​​.
(35)
Since
F′(0)=α>0,F′(K)=α−3βK2=−2α<0,
(36)
the zero equilibrium is unstable and K is asymptotically stable.

b

Words: 62 Articles: 1
6A OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 62
b OurBigBook.com
For 0<n<K, F(n)>0, so solutions increase monotonically toward K. For n>K, F(n)<0, so they decrease monotonically toward K. The solution n=0 remains at zero. Thus a phase-line sketch has arrows away from 0 and toward K; a time-series sketch has all positive curves tending to the same horizontal asymptote K. This is the cubic saturation population model.

c

Words: 83 Articles: 1
6A OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 83
c OurBigBook.com
With the same low-density rate and carrying capacity, the two per-capita growth rates are
nn˙​=α(1−K2n2​)
(37)
for the cubic model and
nn˙​=α(1−Kn​)
(38)
for logistic growth. The logistic correction is linear in a small population, whereas the cubic correction is quadratic. Consequently the cubic trajectory initially follows pure exponential growth more closely and lies above the logistic trajectory before both approach K. Plotting measured per-capita growth against n distinguishes a linear decline from a curve with zero slope at the origin.

a OurBigBook.com
For a received word y, the ideal-observer rule chooses a message i maximizing the posterior probability
P(M=i∣Y=y).
(64)
Maximum-likelihood decoding chooses i maximizing
P(Y=y∣M=i),
(65)
and minimum-distance decoding chooses a codeword minimizing its Hamming distance from y.
Bayes' formula gives
P(M=i∣Y=y)∝P(Y=y∣M=i)P(M=i).
(66)
Equal message priors therefore make ideal-observer and maximum-likelihood decoding identical. On a binary symmetric channel, if d=dH​(y,ci​), then

Two registers suffice. Use register 0 for the input and register 1 as a stack of markers.
The finite control first rejects the empty word. While the next input symbol is a, remove it from register 0 and append one marker to register 1. On seeing the first b, enter a second phase. For every b removed from register 0, remove one marker from register 1; reject if a marker is unavailable or if an a is encountered in this phase. The soundness theorem for propositional logic says that if Γ⊢t, then every valuation satisfying every member of Γ also satisfies t.
The proposed function need not respect the connectives. For example, if a primitive proposition p is independent of S, then neither p nor ¬p is provable from S, so the definition gives
v(p)=v(¬p)=0.
(117)
Order the consistent supersets of S by inclusion. The union of a chain is consistent, since a finite proof of a contradiction would already use assumptions from one member of the chain. Zorn lemma therefore gives a maximal consistent extension T. It is deductively closed: if T⊢t, adjoining t preserves consistency, so maximality forces t∈T. Moreover, for every t, exactly one of t and ¬t belongs to T. They cannot both belong by consistency; if neither belonged, the inconsistency of both proper extensions would give T⊢¬t and T⊢¬¬t, again a contradiction. The usual induction on formulae now shows that
v(t)=1⟺t∈T
(118)
defines a valuation satisfying T, and hence S.
Now suppose every finite subset of S has a model. By soundness every finite subset is consistent. Any proof of a contradiction from S uses only finitely many assumptions, so S itself is consistent. Applying the preceding maximal-consistent-extension construction gives a model of S. This proves the propositional compactness theorem.

and a group element fixing every basis vector must be the identity.

λ,λ2,…,λp−1
(134)
in the spectrum. Therefore dimV≥p−1. This is the spectrum orbit bound for a faithful symmetric-group representation.
Finally let G be the group of all permutations of N. It has no faithful finite-dimensional complex representation. For every n, G contains a subgroup (C2​)n generated by n disjoint transpositions. In a d-dimensional complex representation, commuting involutions are simultaneously diagonalizable and hence map into the group of diagonal sign matrices, which has order 2d. A faithful restriction would require 2n≤2d for every n, an impossibility.

The closest point theorem in a Hilbert space states that every nonempty closed convex subset C of a Hilbert space has a unique point nearest to any given x.
Let d=infy∈C​∥x−y∥ and choose yn​∈C with ∥x−yn​∥→d. The parallelogram identity and convexity give
∥yn​−ym​∥2=2∥x−yn​∥2+2∥x−ym​∥2−4​x−2yn​+ym​​​2≤2∥x−yn​∥2+2∥x−ym​∥2−4d2,
(145)
so (yn​) is Cauchy. Completeness and closedness give a limit y∈C with ∥x−y∥=d. If y,z were both minimizers, the same identity with their midpoint would force ∥y−z∥=0.
Apply the theorem to a closed subspace F. For x∈H, let y∈F be closest and put z=x−y. For every u∈F, minimality of ∥z−tu∥2 at t=0 for real and imaginary t gives ⟨z,u⟩=0. Hence
x=y+z∈F+F⊥.
(146)
The intersection is zero, so H=F⊕F⊥.
If T is a shift with orthonormal basis (en​), it is an isometry,
(ImT)⊥=span{e1​},⋂n≥1​Im(Tn)={0}.
(147)
Conversely, suppose these three properties hold. Choose a unit vector e1​ spanning (ImT)⊥ and set en​=Tn−1e1​. Isometry makes this sequence orthonormal. Iterating the orthogonal decomposition
H=span{e1​}⊕ImT
(148)
gives

(149)
A vector orthogonal to every en​ lies in every Im(Tn) and is therefore zero. Thus (en​) is an orthonormal basis and Ten​=en+1​, so T is a shift. This is the wandering-vector characterization of a unilateral shift.

A covering map is locally a disjoint union of homeomorphisms onto the base. A space is simply connected when it is path-connected and every loop is null-homotopic. By the uniformization theorem, the simply connected Riemann surfaces are
C∞​,C,D
(155)
up to analytic isomorphism.
A lattice is a discrete subgroup
L=Zω1​⊕Zω2​⊂C
(156)
with ω1​/ω2​∈/R. The Weierstrass elliptic function
℘L​(z)=z21​+∑0=ω∈L​((z−ω)21​−ω21​)
(157)
converges normally on compact subsets of C∖L, defines a meromorphic map C→C∞​, and is nonconstant because it has a double pole at every lattice point. Reindexing the normally convergent derivative series shows that ℘L′​ is L-periodic; evenness fixes the integration constants, so ℘L​(z+ω)=℘L​(z).
The invariance makes
℘​([z])=℘L​(z)
(158)
well-defined and unique on C/L. It is analytic because the quotient projection is locally biholomorphic.
Neither map is a covering. For any nonzero ω∈L, periodicity and oddness of ℘L′​ give
℘L′​(ω/2)=℘L′​(−ω/2)=−℘L′​(ω/2),
(159)
so ℘L′​(ω/2)=0. The map is not a local homeomorphism there; since the quotient projection is locally biholomorphic, the descended map fails for the same reason.
There is no covering C/L→C∞​. The torus is connected, while every connected covering of the simply connected sphere is a homeomorphism. A torus is not homeomorphic to a sphere, for example because their fundamental groups are Z2 and 0.

Lorentz invariance requires Aμ and Jμ to transform as four-vectors, χ as a scalar, m and μ0​ as scalars, and the integration domain and boundary conditions to respect the transformation. Then every contracted term and d4x are Lorentz invariant.
Under Aμ​↦Aμ​+∂μ​χ, the field strength is unchanged. The source term changes by a boundary term plus
−∫χ∂μ​Jμ,d4x,

which vanishes for a conserved current and suitable boundary behaviour of χ. The mass term is not gauge invariant. Thus the action has the usual local gauge invariance when
m=0,∂μ​Jμ=0,​
